descript.abstract: Fire can be a significant driver of permafrost change in boreal landscapes, altering the availability of soil carbon and nutrients that have important implications for future climate and ecological succession. However, not all landscapes are equally susceptible to fire-induced change. As fire frequency is expected to increase in the high latitudes, methods to understand the vulnerability and resilience of different landscapes to permafrost degradation are needed. Geophysical and other field observations reveal details of both near-surface (less than 1 m) and deeper (greater than 1 m) impacts of fire on permafrost along 14 transects that span burned-unburned boundaries in different landscape settings within interior Alaska. Electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) data collected along the 14 transect were used to map the spatial distribution of permafrost across burned-unburned boundaries.
descript.purpose: Data were collected to quantify the belowground impacts of fire on permafrost in boreal landscapes.

procstep.procdesc: Spatial locations were determined from a hand-held global positioning system (GPS) device (Ashtech MobileMapper100). Coordinates were recorded in decimal degrees (WGS84).

Electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) transects were acquired using a SuperSting R8 instrument (Advanced Geosciences, Inc., Austin, Texas). Stainless steel electrodes were placed in the ground every 1.5 meters along each transect, and connected to the acquisition instrument through multi-conductor cables and switch boxes. After data were acquired on the first layout of electrodes, transects were extended to their full length using the roll-along method, whereby 28 electrodes at a time were moved from the beginning to the end of the transect and new data were acquired. A dipole-dipole survey geometry was used to acquire each two-dimensional ERT profile, with variable a-spacing (the separation between transmitting electrodes) and maximum n-spacing equal to 8 (the separation between transmitting and receiving electrodes). ERT data were downloaded from the SuperSting R8 instrument and stored digitally.

Data were read into the the EarthImager 2D inversion software (Advanced Geosciences, Inc.; version 2.2.6.554) and merged with the GPS coordinates, including elevation, for each electrode. Spikes and negative apparent resistivity data were removed from the dataset, and preliminary inversions were used to identify other data outliers that were removed using the EarthImager histogram removal tool. Final inversions were run with the edited dataset using the 'Robust' inversion settings, and inverted resistivity models were output when the predicted forward response to final inverted models typically fit measured observations to within 5 – 10%, consistent with expected levels of noise in the ERT data. Resistivity values were stored digitally, along with coordinates and elevations, for each cross-section. Model sensitivity information output from the EarthImager 2D software was used to calculate transparency shading values on a 0-1 scale that can be used to optionally shade resistivity images where model parameters have low sensitivity to the measured data.
ESRI shapefiles of site locations and locations where ERT and NMR data were collected were developed from GPS coordinates recorded in the field. Shapefiles were projected to UTM zone 6 (WGS84).
